chapters.title: Chapter 1: Neural Network and Transformer Fundamentals
chapters.description: Covers the core building blocks of modern large language models (LLMs). Explains transformer architectures, the role of attention and feed‑forward layers, and how linear projections are used throughout the network.
subtopics: Artificial neurons, layers, activations
Transformer architecture: encoder, decoder, and decoder‑only variants
Scaled dot‑product attention and multi‑head attention
Position embeddings and tokenization basics
Feed‑forward/MLP blocks and layer normalization
Typical parameter counts and where parameters are concentrated (e.g., projection matrices)
Forward pass dataflow in a transformer block

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Matrix Computation and Automatic Differentiation
chapters.description: Explains the linear algebra and autodiff that underlie forward and backward passes in deep networks, with emphasis on gradients through linear layers and batched matrix multiplications used in LLMs.
subtopics: Batched matrix multiplication (GEMM) and shapes
Vectorized computation and broadcasting
Chain rule and backpropagation through linear layers
Gradient shapes and how gradients propagate through attention and projections
Computation graph, forward/backward passes, and memory for activations
Jacobian/vector‑Jacobian products and efficient gradient computation

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Numerical Representations and Floating‑Point Formats
chapters.description: Introduces numeric types used in ML: IEEE floats, reduced‑precision formats, and integer/fixed point representations. Discusses tradeoffs in precision, dynamic range, and hardware support.
subtopics: IEEE 754 FP32 and FP64 basics (sign, exponent, mantissa)
FP16, BF16: differences, dynamic range, and precision
Reduced formats (FP8 variants) and custom low‑bit floats
Integers and fixed‑point representations (Int8, Int4)
Rounding modes and numerical error sources
Hardware support: tensor cores, mixed precision compute, and supported types

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Quantization Principles and Techniques
chapters.description: Covers the theory and practice of reducing numeric precision by quantization: uniform and non‑uniform schemes, per‑tensor and per‑block scaling, dequantization, and common algorithms used for LLM weight compression.
subtopics: Definition of quantization and dequantization
Uniform (linear) quantization vs non‑uniform quantization
Per‑tensor, per‑channel, and block‑wise quantization
Absolute‑max (min‑max) scaling and scale factors
Quantization error and bias; handling outliers
Quantile (equal‑probability) quantization and histogram‑based methods
Practical workﬂows: quantize→store→dequantize for inference

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Statistical Properties of Neural Weights and Activations
chapters.description: Discusses empirical distributions of pretrained model weights and activations, common statistical assumptions (e.g., approximate normality), and how these properties impact quantization and scaling choices.
subtopics: Empirical distribution shapes of weights in pretrained networks
Normality assumptions and methods to test for normality
Scale (standard deviation) and mean centering of weight tensors
Outliers and heavy tails in activation distributions
Per‑block statistics and why small block sizes are used
Implications of distributional properties for quantizer design

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Information Theory and Optimal Scalar Quantization
chapters.description: Introduces information‑theoretic concepts relevant to quantization: distortion, rate, optimal quantizers for known distributions, and practical approximations such as Lloyd‑Max and quantile methods.
subtopics: Quantization error (distortion) metrics: MSE, MAE
Rate‑distortion intuition for scalar quantization
Lloyd‑Max algorithm (k‑means for scalars) and optimality conditions
Quantile (equal mass) vs minimum MSE quantizers and when each is appropriate
Effect of source distribution (e.g., Gaussian) on optimal codebook
Tradeoffs between codebook size, bits, and expected distortion

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Parameter‑Efficient Fine‑Tuning and Low‑Rank Adaptation
chapters.description: Explains methods for adapting large pretrained models while changing only a small fraction of parameters. Focuses on the LoRA concept and other PEFT techniques used to reduce compute and memory during finetuning.
subtopics: Motivation for parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning (PEFT)
LoRA: formulation, low‑rank decomposition of updates, and integration into layers
Other PEFT methods: prompt tuning, adapter modules, BitFit, IA3, prefix tuning
Comparison of PEFT approaches: parameter count, memory, and expressivity
How gradients flow when base weights are frozen and only adapters are updated
Practical hyperparameters: rank r, scaling factors, and placement of adapters

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Mixed‑Precision Training and Numerical Stability
chapters.description: Covers training strategies that mix numeric precisions to reduce memory and speed up compute while maintaining numerical stability: master weights, loss scaling, and tradeoffs between compute and storage precision.
subtopics: Mixed precision training workflow (FP32 master + low‑precision compute)
BF16 vs FP16: when and why to use each
Loss scaling techniques to avoid underflow in low precision
Precision considerations for gradient accumulation and optimizer state
Implications for accuracy and convergence
Framework support (PyTorch AMP, automatic casting)

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Optimization Algorithms, States, and Memory Costs
chapters.description: Details common optimizers used for finetuning (Adam, AdamW, SGD variants), the additional state they require, and how optimizer state size contributes to overall memory footprint.
subtopics: Adam, AdamW, SGD with momentum: update rules and hyperparameters
Per‑parameter optimizer states (moment estimates, second moments)
Memory cost breakdown: parameters, gradients, optimizer states, activations
Techniques to reduce optimizer memory: sharding, fp16 states, state offloading
Effect of batch size and sequence length on optimizer and activation memory

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Memory Management for Large‑Scale Training on GPUs
chapters.description: Explains GPU memory management issues faced when training large models: activation storage, gradient checkpointing, memory spikes, and strategies to fit models on limited GPU RAM including CPU‑GPU memory movement techniques.
subtopics: GPU memory hierarchy and capacity constraints
Activation memory and why sequence length matters
Gradient checkpointing (activation recomputation) to trade compute for memory
Sharding and model parallelism approaches (tensor/split sharding)
Offloading optimizer states to CPU RAM and host/device transfers
CUDA Unified Memory basics and page migration concepts (OS‑level paging)

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Efficient Inference and Quantized Inference Methods
chapters.description: Surveys inference‑focused quantization and accuracy‑preserving tricks developed to run large models efficiently at low precision, including ways to handle outlier channels and grouped scaling.
subtopics: Per‑channel and per‑block scaling for inference quantization
SmoothQuant and other methods to move outlier scaling between activations and weights
GPTQ and post‑training quantization for LLMs
Grouped and block quantization strategies and their tradeoffs
Hybrid precision inference (keeping some tensors in higher precision)
Evaluation of quantized models: perplexity and downstream task performance

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Evaluation Methodologies for Language Models and Chatbots
chapters.description: Presents common benchmarks and evaluation methodologies used to assess LLMs and chatbots, plus statistical considerations for human and model‑based evaluations.
subtopics: Standard benchmarks: GLUE, MMLU, Super‑NaturalInstructions and others
Instruction following and chatbot evaluation datasets (Vicuna prompts, OASST1, etc.)
Human annotation protocols: pairwise comparisons, rating scales, inter‑annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa)
Model‑based evaluation using stronger LMs as judges (pros/cons and known biases)
Tournament/pairwise evaluation and Elo rating systems for model ranking
Confidence intervals, bootstrapping, and reporting variability in results

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Instruction Fine‑Tuning, Distillation, and RLHF (Overview)
chapters.description: Describes the different supervised and reinforcement learning approaches to adapt LLMs to follow instructions and behave as chatbots, including data sources and training objectives commonly used.
subtopics: Supervised instruction finetuning with cross‑entropy loss
Data sources: human‑created dialogs, model distillation, crowdsourced instruction datasets
Knowledge distillation and self‑instruct methods
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF): components and motivation
Differences in objectives and their effects on behavior
Practical considerations for multi‑turn dialog training and prompt formatting

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Low‑Level GPU Programming and Kernel Development Basics
chapters.description: Introduces relevant GPU programming concepts for implementing custom low‑bit kernels and efficient matrix routines: CUDA programming model, memory coalescing, warp execution, and profiling basics.
subtopics: CUDA programming model: threads, blocks, warps, kernels
Memory types: global, shared, constant, registers, and their performance characteristics
Coalesced memory access, occupancy, and avoiding bank conflicts
Implementing custom matmul kernels and low‑bit compute kernels (conceptual overview)
Tooling and profiling: nvprof, Nsight, and GPU performance counters
Interfacing custom kernels with deep learning frameworks (PyTorch extensions)

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Experimental Design, Reproducibility, and Statistical Analysis
chapters.description: Covers best practices for designing experiments with large models, performing controlled ablations, hyperparameter searches, and reporting reproducible comparative results with appropriate statistical rigor.
subtopics: Designing controlled experiments and ablation studies
Hyperparameter search strategies and generalization across scales
Measuring runtime, memory, and throughput reliably
Statistical tests, confidence intervals, and multiple comparisons
Reproducibility: seeds, environment, and deterministic issues
Reporting guidelines for benchmarks and open release practices
